context_blurb:
Every living thing needs food, and nearly every living thing is food for something else. Grass feeds a rabbit, and the rabbit feeds a fox. Follow these links through a meadow, a pond or the open sea, and you find that they tie everything together, so a change to one member is felt by many others.

Every food chain starts with a producer, a living thing that makes its own food. Green plants and algae are producers, powered by the Sun's light. Even the moss on a forest rock is a producer, because moss is a small green plant, and like other plants it makes its own food from sunlight. A mushroom may look like a plant, but it is a fungus. It cannot make food, so it feeds on dead wood and leaves, as one of the decomposers. Animals such as snails and beetles are consumers: they must eat other living things.

Consumers are named for what they eat. A herbivore is a plant-eater, and a wild rabbit is a true one, living on grass, leaves, bark and twigs and nothing else. Deer and most caterpillars are herbivores too. A carnivore eats other animals. In a field, grasshoppers eat grass, frogs eat grasshoppers, and snakes eat frogs. Both the frog and the snake are carnivores, because both eat animals. It does not matter that the frog is eaten in its turn. The grasshopper eats plants, so it is a herbivore.

An omnivore eats both plants and animals, as bears and people do. In a forest where mice eat seeds and also caterpillars, the mice are omnivores, since seeds come from plants and caterpillars are animals. There, the deer and caterpillars eat only plants, and the owls eat only animals.

On paper, a food chain is a line of living things joined by arrows: grass → rabbit → fox. Each arrow points toward the living thing that eats, showing which way the food's energy travels. Many students draw the arrows backwards, so read each one as "is eaten by". The eater is not always bigger, either: a wolf pack can bring down a moose several times heavier than any one wolf.

A real pond is messier than one chain, because few animals stick to one kind of food. Frogs snap up many kinds of insects, and both snakes and herons hunt frogs. All the food chains of one place, joined where they overlap, make up a food web. Overlapping chains form a web, not one longer chain.

In a web, a change to one member spreads far. Picture a marsh where herons hunt frogs, and frogs eat the insects that chew the plants. Then a sickness wipes out nearly all the frogs. With the frogs gone, hardly anything eats the insects, so the insects multiply and there are more insects than before. They eat more of the plants, and the herons, short of food, dwindle.

The links pull both ways. If far more rabbits than usual are born in a meadow one spring, they eat the grass faster than it can grow back, so less of it is left. Grass makes its own food and regrows, but not fast enough for so many hungry mouths.

Far out at sea, where the water is miles deep, light reaches only the top part, so producers must live near the surface. Most of the ocean's producers are tiny floating algae called phytoplankton, each too small to see on its own, drifting in the sunlit water. Tiny drifting animals, which are consumers, graze on them. No seaweed grows on the dark seabed miles down, and the few floating seaweed mats make only a small share of the ocean's food.
